title: These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out
gist: Three Axiom engineers got OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, a text model, to drive a Toyota Corolla to an In-N-Out drive-thru with no special training, a sign that language models are gaining rudimentary physical understanding. Their DrivingBench shows only Astra completes a simple parking-lot course, and slowly, while other labs and startups push on physical reasoning for robotics.

insights.claim: Axiom engineers connected cameras and power steering to a chat interface and had OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, a general text model, drive a 2024 Corolla to an In-N-Out take-out window on the fly with no prior coaching, with a safety driver ready.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Demonstrates general-purpose models can be coaxed into real-world control, widening the AI-safety and robotics surface.

insights.claim: Language-based models are starting to show a rudimentary but useful understanding of the physical world, per the fast-food stunt and other experiments.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Physical reasoning is a next capability frontier relevant to robotics and autonomy exposure.

insights.claim: Models initially refused to issue motion commands to a physical car but could be coaxed into driving with careful prompting.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Refusal guardrails are prompt-bypassable, a safety and liability risk.
insights.quote: I can help interpret road images, but I can’t issue motion commands to a physical car.
insights.locator: The engineers tried testing SpaceXAI’s Grok

insights.claim: The engineers think driving ability likely emerged from 3D-reasoning and multimodal training rather than deliberate driving training, suggesting it scales with multimodality.
insights.speaker: Simon Mahns
insights.so_what: If emergent from scaling multimodality, physical skills may arrive across labs without targeted effort.
insights.quote: This could be like an emergent capability of just scaling up the multimodality of the model
insights.locator: The engineers say big AI companies seem

insights.claim: On the new DrivingBench parking-lot course only GPT-6 Astra finishes, very slowly; Claude Fable 5.1 reaches 45 percent and Grok 11 percent.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Models remain far from passing a driving test, so autonomy via general LLMs is not near-term.

insights.claim: Models appeared to adapt to the car's controls and improve in real time, which Ramabadran reads as in-context learning from mistakes.
insights.speaker: Aditya Ramabadran
insights.so_what: Test-time adaptation is a possible route to physical competence without retraining.
insights.quote: The models really did seem to be adjusting or in-context learning based on their mistakes
insights.locator: Ramabadran says the latest models seem capable

insights.claim: Despite claims AGI has arrived, AI companies evidently see physical reasoning as a yet-to-be-conquered frontier; today's models are strong at questions and virtual tasks but get befuddled in the real world.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Physical AI remains an open problem and potential differentiator.
insights.locator: Today’s smartest models are incredibly good

insights.claim: Ex-DeepMind researcher Andrew Dai runs Elorian AI, a startup built around physical reasoning, and says better visual reasoning unlocks applications like home robots.
insights.speaker: Andrew Dai
insights.so_what: Talent is leaving big labs to found physical-AI startups, a funding theme to watch.
insights.quote: You can’t really imagine home robotics without this.
insights.locator: Some researchers have left big companies

insights.claim: Elorian and Scale AI built the Humanity's Sixth Sense benchmark to test whether models intuitively understand physical scenes rather than just perceive them.
insights.speaker: Xingang Guo
insights.so_what: New benchmarks will define how progress in physical reasoning is measured.
insights.quote: Most visual AI research is about perception
